steps.instruction: This is a TypeScript program. It prints one line.
body: console.log prints. The text in quotes is what comes out.
Java writes System.out.println. TypeScript writes console.log. Same job, shorter.

steps.after: Whatever is in the quotes comes out exactly.

steps.instruction: A variable holds a value. let makes one.
body: No type is written. TypeScript reads 0 and decides score holds numbers.
score = 10 works, because 10 is a number.
steps.keypoint: let name = value; — TypeScript works out the type from the value.

steps.instruction: Add a line that sets score to the text "ten". Do not run anything — watch what happens as you type.
steps.after: You never pressed Run. TypeScript already knew.

body: score was set to 0, so TypeScript decided it holds numbers.
Java would tell you this too — but only after you compiled it.
steps.keypoint: Once a variable has a type, it keeps it.

steps.instruction: Declare name holding "Ada" and city holding "Markham". Print name, then city.
steps.hint: let name = "Ada"; then a console.log for each.

steps.instruction: const holds a value that never changes.
body: let can be reassigned later. const cannot.
Use const unless you know the value has to change.
steps.keypoint: const for values that stay put, let for values that change.

steps.instruction: This will not compile. Change one word so it does.
steps.hint: count changes, so it cannot be const.
steps.after: count changes value, so it needs let.

steps.why: b is const, so it cannot be given a new value. a is let, so a = 7 is fine.

steps.instruction: One console.log can print several values.
body: A space is put between them automatically.
steps.keypoint: console.log(a, b) prints both, separated by a space.

steps.after: city never changes, so const. visits does, so let.

steps.instruction: Declare three constants: a string, a number, and true or false. Print all three on one line.
steps.hint: const name = "Ada"; const age = 15; const student = true; then one console.log with all three.
steps.after: Three types, one line. TypeScript worked out all three without being told.

steps.instruction: Write a program that stores a name and a score, then prints them on separate lines.
steps.after: That is a whole TypeScript program.
